solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: For example, straight pointer

definitions.meaning: a straight is five cards in sequence, one kind of holding in poker
the pointer on a clock face

explanation.surface: Someone giving an example of a straight pointer, like a ruler or a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: In poker a straight is one kind of HAND, so 'for example, straight' defines it by giving an instance; a clock's HAND is a pointer.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight is an example of a poker hand, and a clock hand points at the time.

clue.text: On a trip, extensive service

parts.note: on a drug trip, you are high

explanation.surface: Someone on a long journey who attends a lengthy church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a trip' reads as travelling, but here it is the drug sense.
explanation.definitionFit: High Mass is a full, sung Catholic church service.

clue.text: People catching up to score?

indicators.note: the people word holds the other piece inside it
in a down clue, 'up' turns TO backwards

parts.note: used as it stands, then turned to OT

explanation.surface: A crowd of fans racing to catch up with the score of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' suggests sport, but here it is written music; the question mark flags that notation is only one example of a score.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a composer's score is one kind of written system of symbols for music, the question mark admitting it is only one case.

clue.text: Site office left — otherwise, dump

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
to bin something is to dump it

explanation.surface: A building-site office abandoned, or else thrown on the tip.
explanation.walkthrough: A Portakabin is a British brand of portable cabin, the standard temporary office on building sites.
explanation.definitionFit: A Portakabin is the prefabricated hut used as an office on a building site.

clue.text: Delegate exposed cause

parts.note: a secret that is exposed is out
the cause of something is its source

explanation.surface: A conference delegate who has revealed what caused a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delegate' looks like a noun, a person at a conference, but it is the verb: to hand work to someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To outsource a job is to delegate it to an outside firm.

clue.text: Stay or go, crossing a river

indicators.note: the word for 'go' spans across the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: have a go = have a try

explanation.surface: Someone deciding whether to stay put or cross a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay or go' reads as a dilemma, but 'go' is a noun here, as in 'have a go'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain, slightly old-fashioned synonym: to linger somewhere rather than leave is to stay on.

clue.text: 21 in miniature?

parts.note: the surface pushes the 1960s art movement; the setter means the first two letters as short for operation, so the art of the op
not a tiny painting but a procedure done through very small incisions

explanation.surface: An example of 1960s optical art on a tiny scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is OP ART, which reads as the art of the op, or operation; keyhole surgery is that art practised through tiny incisions.
explanation.definitionFit: Keyhole surgery is an operation done through very small openings, surgery in miniature.

clue.text: Song and dance over a daughter

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A parent making a big fuss, a song and dance, about their daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song and dance' is a fuss, but it splits: 'Song' is the definition and 'dance' starts the wordplay. In a down clue, 'over' puts BALL above A D.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballad is a song, usually one that tells a story.

clue.text: Reject any changes eg

indicators.note: the letters of ANY are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to refuse any amendments, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eg' looks like the clue's own aside, but it is a piece of wordplay meaning SAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to refuse or deny something, literally by saying 'nay' to it.

clue.text: Tom Cruise in top flying films

indicators.note: the letters are sent flying and land in a new order

explanation.surface: Tom Cruise flying jets in Top Gun and other films.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Top Gun, where Cruise plays a fighter pilot; the actor's name is only raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the formal, rather dated term for cinema movies.

clue.text: Go the wrong way on your bike

explanation.surface: A cyclist riding off in the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your bike' is British slang for 'go away', which is also what 'get lost' means.
explanation.definitionFit: To get lost is to go the wrong way, and 'get lost!' is a rude dismissal like 'on your bike!'.

clue.text: Rob partner in a big way

parts.note: Rob Roy, the Scottish outlaw: Roy is Rob's partner in the name

explanation.surface: An accomplice helping to commit a robbery on a grand scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rob' looks like a verb, to steal, but it is a name; Rob Roy was an 18th-century Scottish outlaw.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something royally is to do it in a big way, as in 'royally messed up'.

clue.text: Many about to reduce love in wedlock

indicators.note: the word for 'many' goes around the other pieces

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, and nil looks like O

explanation.surface: Many married people trying to cut back on love, a gloomy view of marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' is not a quantity here but letters used as they stand, split open to take the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are formal words for the state of being married.

clue.text: Over in Utah, a modern US city

indicators.note: the letters are read turned over, right to left
the answer sits inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters from utAH A MOdern, then turned round

explanation.surface: A modern American city lying across the state line in Utah.
explanation.walkthrough: Omaha is in Nebraska, not Utah: the state is only a container for the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: it is the largest city in Nebraska, on the Missouri River.

clue.text: Socialite using compass in New Orleans

indicators.note: the word for 'compass' goes inside the other letters
the letters of ORLEANS are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: the compass of a voice or instrument is its range

explanation.surface: A party-goer finding their way round New Orleans with a compass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Orleans' looks like the city, but 'New' is the instruction to rearrange ORLEANS. A Sloane Ranger is a stereotyped upper-class young Londoner, named after Sloane Square in Chelsea.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sloane Ranger is a well-off, fashionable young socialite from west London.

clue.text: Welcome tips after turning in Warhol et al

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so the word before it is read back to front

parts.note: a ship that tips to one side lists

explanation.surface: Gallery visitors welcomed, with advice, at a Warhol exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like advice, but it is the verb for leaning over. Calling Warhol a nihilist is a contestable view of Pop Art's cool emptiness, not a textbook label.
explanation.definitionFit: Warhol's deadpan, surface-only art is often read as nihilistic, so he and like-minded artists can be called nihilists.

clue.text: No fitter state, Jagger assumes

indicators.note: Jagger's name takes on, and holds, the other word

parts.note: Mick Jagger of the Rolling Stones
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: Mick Jagger declaring that he is past his physical best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No fitter' reads as 'not in better shape', but it means someone who does not fit in.
explanation.definitionFit: A maverick is an independent person who does not fit in with the group.

clue.text: Sticking fan

definitions.meaning: the adjective: clinging fast to a surface
the noun: a devoted follower of a cause or person

explanation.surface: A fan whose blades keep jamming.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective means sticking to a surface; the noun means a follower.
explanation.definitionFit: Adherent means sticking fast, and an adherent is a devoted supporter, a fan.

clue.text: Multitude possibly fed Hovis and tuna

indicators.note: what follows is only one possible arrangement of the letters, so try others

explanation.surface: A huge crowd served bread and fish, a modern-brand retelling of a miracle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also reads straight: in the Gospels Jesus feeds a multitude with loaves and fishes, and Hovis is a British bread brand.
explanation.definitionFit: The feeding of the five thousand is the Bible's multitude fed on bread and fish.

clue.text: Bird brains supporting idol

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece supporting another sits beneath it, so the brains word goes second

explanation.surface: A bird-brained person who worships an idol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird brains' reads as an insult, but it splits: 'Bird' is the definition and 'brains' the start of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The godwit is a long-billed wading bird.

clue.text: Call from hunting lobby reaching ducks

parts.note: an entrance hall is a lobby
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so two ducks are two Os

explanation.surface: The pro-hunting lobby's cry going as far as the ducks on the pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunting lobby' looks like a pressure group, but 'lobby' is the room.
explanation.definitionFit: Halloo is the shout used to urge on hounds in hunting.

clue.text: Old quarter's newer design

parts.note: a quarter is a part of the whole

explanation.surface: An old district of a city getting a modern redesign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' and 'newer' seem to clash, which is the joke: the old part yields a newer style.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is a 1960s style of abstract design using optical illusions, newer than most art movements.

clue.text: Italian medic about to register drug

indicators.note: the medic word goes around the next piece

parts.note: Bones is slang for a doctor, from sawbones

explanation.surface: An Italian doctor about to prescribe a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' works alone as the container and 'to' just adds the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: someone from the city of Bologna is one kind of Italian.

clue.text: Not even a politician will block bribe

indicators.note: the politician sits in the middle of the other word, blocking it

parts.note: to bribe someone is to buy them

explanation.surface: A politician refusing even to stand in the way of a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even a politician' reads as 'not a single politician', but 'Not even' is the definition: uneven.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a surface full of lumps is uneven, which is what 'not even' spells out.

clue.text: Metal flux around hammer

explanation.surface: A metalworker using flux around a hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: Flux is also a substance used in metalworking, which keeps the surface in the forge.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolfram is another name for tungsten, a metal.

clue.text: Fancy young lady's cut in very well

indicators.note: the shortened word goes inside the next one

parts.note: a young lady is a miss; cut to MIS

explanation.surface: A young woman who fancies someone, well and truly smitten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy young lady' reads as an elegant woman, but 'Fancy' is the verb: to suppose.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to suppose or guess, as in 'I fancy it will rain'.

clue.text: Radical, corrupt broadcaster is in Times

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the letters for 'Times'

parts.note: T is time, so two Ts for 'Times'

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a crooked broadcaster exposed in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, but it is just two Ts. Sky is a British satellite TV broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trotskyist, a follower of Leon Trotsky, is a radical left-winger.

clue.text: Saint Christopher caricature

parts.note: Kit is a short form of Christopher

explanation.surface: A cartoon of St Christopher, patron saint of travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Christopher' reads as one name, but it splits into S and Christopher, shortened to KIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A skit is a short comic sketch that caricatures its subject.
